newsitem.title: EGYPT: Mideast meeting focuses on business not politics.
newsitem.headline: Mideast meeting focuses on business not politics.

text.p: Hopes dimmed on Monday that this week's Middle East economic conference would showcase an announcement of an Israel-PLO deal on the long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank town of Hebron.
Instead, officials were hailing the business opportunities at the three-day Middle East/North Africa meeting starting on Tuesday.
There were hopes the conference, grouping more than 2,000 business people from some 80 countries, would provide the fitting backdrop for announcement of a Hebron agreement.

But a Palestinian negotiator said the two sides were unlikely to reach a deal at the meeting on the partial Israeli pullout, delayed since March. Arab leaders and peace envoys were also far from hopeful.

"My personal impression from (Egyptian President Hosni) Mubarak and from meeting (Foreign Minister Amr) Moussa was that they are not over-optimistic on this," said Japan's Middle East envoy, Nobuo Matsunaga.
"I think we will have to be patient," he told reporters.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is not attending the conference. Palestinian President Yasser Arafat will meet outgoing U.S. Foreign Secretary Warren Christopher in Cairo on Tuesday, but Arafat also had no plans to attend.

But the stalled peace process, snagged on Israel's demand to modify a previous Hebron accord and tighten security for the 400 Jews living amid 100,000 Palestinians in the town, failed to undermine the optimism of the conference's backers.

Only a few months ago Egypt was so angry with Netanyahu's uncompromising stance in the peace talks that it threatened to cancel the conference, the third such regional gathering since the Middle East peace process was launched in Madrid in 1991.
It soon saw there was too much to lose.
"Public and private business investors will come to see Egypt's investment capabilities," said the government newspaper Al-Akhbar. "It is a golden opportunity to showcase Egypt's new economy."

As with the previous two conferences, regional governments will be presenting a billion-dollar wish list of projects whose size dwarfs many of the underdeveloped economies of the Middle East as well as their tiny capital markets.

Many of these projects are likely to remain on the drawing board but officials emphasise that the conference is nevertheless crucial for a region largely seen as a battlefield rather than a stable ground for business.
"This conference is important economically and for the peace process," said French Finance and Foreign Trade Minister Yves Galland on his arrival at the head of a delegation of 50 business people.
Most of the conference sessions, largely chaired by U.S. officials or senior corporate executives, focus on breaking down the barriers to business in the region and to promoting growth.
A minority of the planned panels deal with any of the region's thornier issues.

A session scheduled on water looks at desalination and resource management. There is no mention of water rights in the programme which is a point of contention between Palestinians and Israelis as well as between other regional states.
The programme of another session poses a question reflecting the tensions in Arab-Israeli relations: "Does economic integration between Israel and the Palestinians make sense?"
